title: Temporal link variance mapping with histogrammed pings
content:
Summary:

This scratchpad describes a lightweight, reproducible methodology for mapping temporal variance on interconnect links (NVLink/PCIe/NIC) using histogrammed ping traces and correlating those micro-variance signatures with pipeline/tensor-parallel tail latency in LLM inference. The goal is to produce an actionable fingerprint per-rack / per-node that helps scheduler placement and fallback policies.

Motivation / background:
- We keep seeing sporadic tail latency spikes (~95th-99.9th) for multi-GPU TP/PP deployments that don’t reproduce on synthetic steady-state loads.
- Hypothesis: transient link noise (microbursts, arbitration delays, NIC interrupts) causes small, infrequent stalls that amplify across synchronous collectives and serialized pipeline boundaries.
- Existing probes (iperf, synthetic allreduce) capture throughput but miss short-duration variance. Need an instrumentation designed to capture millisecond-to-microsecond level jitter frequency distribution.

Experiment overview:
1) Run a lightweight histogrammed-ping agent on all relevant host interfaces (nvlink counters exposed via nvidia-smi/nvlink probes, PCIe TLP latency probes where available, and NIC per-queue micro RTTs).
2) Collect high-resolution timestamps across 30–90 minute windows during both idle background and during a controlled inference burst workload (real model with realistic seq-length distribution).
3) Correlate histogram signatures (skew, kurtosis, heavy tails, burst count) with per-request token-latency traces from the runtime (we already emit per-token timing).
4) Identify reproducible fingerprints and quantify impact on tail latency percentiles.

Environment / infra details:
- Cluster: rack-a (4 nodes), each node: 8x A100s (HGX-like), NVSwitch disabled in these runs (typical host NVLink topology, mixed 3-hop rings).
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04 + CUDA 12.2, driver 535.x, NCCL 2.15.6.
- Runtime build: main@serving-runtime with inlined per-token tracing (PR 481).
- Workload: opt-6.7b baseline, TP=2, PP=2 for 8-GPU placement (2 replicas), batch=1 with mixed request distribution (short/medium/long contexts).
- Measurement agents: small Python harness using perf counter reads + ethtool timestamping where supported. Histogram bins: microsecond buckets up to 2ms, then logarithmic bins to 50ms.

Instrumentation notes:
- On NVLink: nvlink counters are read every 250us; we record per-link transfer start/end events via a lightweight kernel-level probe where possible (falls back to aggregated counters otherwise).
- On PCIe: host-side TLP latency sampling via existing platform PMU events (not universal).
- NIC: use ethtool hw timestamping + per-queue ring occupancy logs; release IRQ affinity toggles in different runs.
- Synchronization: all agents are synced from a host NTP stratum; for microsecond-level alignment we also record a local monotonic counter and perform drift alignment in postprocessing.

Experiment runs performed:
- run-2025-11-17-01: idle background (no model load) for 60 minutes — baseline link histograms.
- run-2025-11-17-02: steady synthetic allreduce (large tensors) for 30 minutes — tests throughput stable ring behavior.
- run-2025-11-17-03: realistic inference burst (peak QPS ~200 for short contexts) for 45 minutes — collect token traces and link histograms.
- run-2025-11-17-04: replica placement variant (move one replica to cross-rack node) to test inter-rack link effect.

Representative findings (summary numbers, aggregated across 4 nodes):
- Baseline idle histograms: 99% of NVLink transfer RTs < 20us, but ~0.6% of events in 50–200us tail (microbursts).
- Synthetic allreduce: very low variance (<0.05% > 50us) when rings are saturated (large payloads) — i.e., steady-state collectives mask microbursts.
- Real inference burst: distinct heavy-tail emerges — 95th=22us, 99th=62us, 99.9th=370us for NVLink transfers correlated with token stalls.
- Cross-rack placement: NIC per-queue jitter increases 99.9th to ~1.1ms and strongly correlates with pipeline cutpoint stalls when data shuffles are required across replicas.

Key correlations observed:
- Token-level per-request stalls consistently follow a NVLink microburst within 5–10ms window (likely due to collective backpressure and re-ordering inside the ring).
- Pipeline boundaries (PP stage handoff) amplify link variance by factor ~3–5x in observed token stall durations vs. single collective latency because pending KV-cache transfers block dependent layers.
- NCCL fallbacks / reconfigurations (observed in logs) correlate with longer tails — when NCCL switches topology unexpectedly on degraded link signals, we saw 2x frequency of 99.9th spikes.

Concrete example (annotated event sequence):
- t=12.420 s: NVLinkA link trace shows a 180us transfer event (outlier).
- t=12.425 s: NCCL logs a delayed allreduce completion on rank 3 (40us extra), start of re-send window.
- t=12.426 s: runtime trace token: layer 23 wait 0.15ms -> downstream pipeline stage waits for KV flush -> request token latency jumped from median 18ms to 19.2ms (per-token delta 1.2ms).

Interpretation / what this means for scheduling and runtime policies:
- Small-probability microbursts are benign for throughput but can create disproportionate tail latency due to synchronous collectives and serialized pipeline dependencies.
- Scheduler should prefer soft-affinity that groups strongly communicating PP/TP stages across links with low histogram tail mass; prefer intra-node NVSwitch islands when a node supports it.
- Runtime can mitigate by: enabling per-collective slack (adaptive timeout leveling), opportunistic local replica fallback (serve degraded with slower model variant), and preemptive KV-cache replication for high tail-sensitivity routes.

Immediate recommendations (engineering action items):
- Add a lightweight histogrammed-ping agent to cluster health checks (low overhead, 1 sample every 200us aggregated into minute buckets). Jira: JIRA-INVEST-712. Owner: Marcus.
- Expose a per-link 'tail score' in node metadata consumed by the scheduler (computed daily and on-demand during incidents).
- In runtime, add a probation policy that detects NCCL topology reconfig events and temporarily enforces per-request fallback to local quantized variant for a small percentage of traffic. RFC PR: github PR 481 (experimental).

Next experiments / unknowns:
- Validate on NVSwitch-enabled nodes; current tests used non-NVSwitch configurations — suspicion is NVSwitch reduces microburst coupling but may introduce its own shared-bus interference.
- Repeat with ECC on vs off; memory ECC correction latencies may add rare long tails.
- Test different NCCL versions (2.14, 2.16) to measure reconfiguration frequency sensitivity.

Notes / rough commands used:
- histogram agent (pseudo):
  python tools/histogram_ping.py --interface nvlink0 --sample-interval-us 250 --duration-min 60 --bins config/hist-bins.json --out /tmp/hist-run-01.json
- runtime traces: per-token tracing toggled via env var TRACE_PER_TOKEN=1 and collected via s3 logs for postprocessing.
- small-aggregation: jq + python to align monotonic counters and compute per-bin counts.

Open questions for discussion in sync:
- Threshold choice: what % of tail (99.9th) should drive automatic replica failover? 0.05%? 0.1%? We need SLO-guided thresholds.
- Tradeoff between reactive NCCL reconfigs vs proactive placement changes — reconfigs reduce bandwidth contention but add coordination noise.
- Operational cost: how often to run histogram scans cluster-wide without adding measurement noise?

Appendix: quick visuals (handwritten notes) — will generate CSVs and upload to Confluence. Sample CSV columns: timestamp, node, link, bin_upper_us, count, inferred-tail-pct.
